clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of mitochondrial 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate aldolase (HOGA1), part of the hydroxyproline degradation pathway
Biochemical signature is raised urinary oxalate together with elevated 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate and 2,4-dihydroxyglutarate, separating it from the glycolate of type 1 and L-glycerate of type 2
Often has the earliest age of first stone among the primary hyperoxalurias, frequently in infancy or early childhood
Paradoxically tends to have the mildest long-term course, with symptomatic stone episodes that may diminish with age
Progression to chronic kidney disease and systemic oxalosis is uncommon, although it has been reported and cannot be assumed absent
Diagnosis relies on urinary oxalate with the specific metabolite profile and confirmation by HOGA1 gene sequencing
Management is generic and supportive with vigorous hyperhydration and urinary crystallisation inhibitors such as citrate; there is no enzyme replacement
Hepatic lactate dehydrogenase-directed RNA-interference therapy is being studied across the primary hyperoxaluria subtypes
reference.pathophysiology: HOGA1 normally cleaves 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate, an intermediate of hydroxyproline catabolism, within the mitochondrion. Its deficiency causes accumulation of 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate and its derivative 2,4-dihydroxyglutarate; the accumulated substrate is thought to be diverted to glyoxylate and then oxidised to oxalate, and loss of a normal inhibitory influence on glyoxylate handling may contribute further. The resulting oxalate overproduction promotes calcium oxalate crystallisation in the urinary tract, causing stones and, less commonly than in the other types, nephrocalcinosis and renal impairment.
additionalDifferentials: Hypercalciuric and other metabolic stone-forming states
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative urinary oxalate excretion with organic-acid profiling for 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate and 2,4-dihydroxyglutarate
Renal tract ultrasound for calculi and nephrocalcinosis
Estimation of glomerular filtration rate and urinary citrate
Plasma oxalate if renal function becomes impaired
redFlags: Neonatal or early infantile presentation with dense nephrocalcinosis
Unexpected decline in glomerular filtration rate despite the usually benign course
Recurrent obstructing calculi causing acute kidney injury
reference.prognosis: Overall the most favourable of the primary hyperoxalurias, with preserved renal function in the majority and stone activity that often lessens over time, though occasional progression means continued monitoring is prudent.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis because standard metabolic screens may not report the specific hydroxyglutarate metabolites
Assuming the benign reputation guarantees a benign outcome in every patient
Attributing recurrent paediatric stones to idiopathic disease without genetic testing
Neglecting hydration advice during febrile illness or reduced intake
references: Belostotsky R et al. Mutations in HOGA1 cause primary hyperoxaluria type III
Cochat P, Rumsby G. Primary hyperoxaluria. New England Journal of Medicine
management: Generous fluid intake to lower urinary calcium oxalate saturation as the mainstay of conservative care
Potassium citrate to increase urinary citrate and inhibit calcium oxalate crystallisation
Moderate dietary oxalate while maintaining adequate calcium intake with meals to reduce enteric oxalate absorption
Treat symptomatic stones with minimally invasive clearance techniques
Periodic surveillance of urinary oxalate, glomerular filtration rate and renal tract ultrasound, since progression is uncommon but cannot be assumed absent
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and family screening
